notes:
I've put together notes on Psalm 134 below. Most of the material is older Protestant commentary (Spurgeon, Calvin, Gill, Matthew Henry, the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott). I found nothing on this psalm from Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan or Orthodox sources, from the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey, or from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers, so those are left out. I also found no real disagreement between traditions on these verses. The commentators differ on smaller points, which I mark as they come up.

**Background: who is speaking to whom?**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) reads the psalm as a call to the temple's priests and Levites to keep praising God, with a blessing sent back to the people. He cites Spurgeon's picture of pilgrims leaving Jerusalem before dawn and calling out to the priests on night watch. It is a call to the priests and Levites of the temple to continue their service of praise, with the answer of a blessing back to the people. Charles Spurgeon suggested that the scene was of pilgrims departing Jerusalem in the darkness of early morning, calling out to the priests and Levites who stood watch at the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-134/
- The Pulpit Commentary suggests the opposite timing: pilgrims arriving late at the temple gates, with the people inside asking God to bless them (v. 3). The psalm is very suitable for pilgrim-bands arriving, as they commonly would, late in the day at the temple gates https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-134.html
- Keil and Delitzsch (quoted on Bible Hub) mention Tholuck's idea that it was sung back and forth as one night watch handed over to the next. They themselves prefer to read verses 1–2 as the congregation calling the night ministers to prayer and to pray for them. Tholuck, with Kster, regards Psalm 134:1. and Psalm 134:3 as the antiphon of the Temple-watch going off duty and those coming on. It might also be the call and counter-call with which the watchmen greeted one another when they met. But according to the general keeping of the Psalm, Psalm 134:1. have rather to be regarded as a call to devotion and intercession, which the congregation addresses to the priests and Levites entrusted with the night-service in the Temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/134-2.htm

**v. 1**
- **"Come" / "Behold":** Adam Clarke takes the Hebrew word (*hinneh*) as a warning: "take heed." I believe הנה hinneh should be taken here in the sense of take heed! Be upon your guard; you serve a jealous God; provoke him not. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/134-1.html Spurgeon hears the departing pilgrims shouting to wake up the watchmen. Their departing brethren arouse them with the shrill cry of "Behold!" Behold!—see, take care, be on the watch, diligently mind your work, and incessantly adore and bless Jehovah's name. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps134.cfm
- **"Bless the LORD":** Guzik explains that people cannot give God a blessing the way a greater person blesses a lesser one. Rather, God is honoured when his creatures rightly praise and thank him. God is infinitely greater than man, and man could never give a blessing to God. The idea is that it blesses and honors God when His creatures praise Him and thank Him appropriately. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-134/
- **"Servants of the LORD":** Most commentators take this to mean the priests and Levites. The Cambridge Bible says it is not worshippers in general, because "stand before the LORD" was the standard phrase for temple ministry. Not Israelite worshippers in general, but, as the following clause shews, ministrants in the Temple. which by night stand in the house of the Lord] 'To stand before Jehovah' was the regular term for priestly or Levitical ministration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/134-1.htm
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) says it could mean either the Levites on night duty or the whole worshipping community, though the second half of the verse points to the Levites. This phrase may be understood, either as the Levites keeping the night vigil in the Temple, or as the "community at worship." Either meaning could be correct. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/134-3.html
- **"By night":** Spurgeon's collected notes describe what the night priests did and the dangers they faced. Those priests renewed the altar fire, fed the lamps, and guarded the sacred structure from intrusion and from plunder. The Psalm before us was prepared for the priests who served the sacred place by night. They were in danger of slumbering; and they were in danger of idle reverie. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps134.cfm Gill records Jewish tradition that the watchmen had to stand, and that priests kept watch in three places and Levites in twenty-one. The priests watched in three places, and the Levites in twenty one, according to the Jewish Misnah https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-134.html
- **Calvin (Reformed):** The point is that keeping watch and doing the rituals was worth nothing without real, heartfelt praise. Some Levites thought just standing in the temple was enough. Many of the Levites, through the tendency which there is in all men to abuse ceremonies, considered that nothing more was necessary than standing idly in the Temple, and thus overlooked the principal part of their duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-134.html
- **Application to Christians today:** Gill says that under the gospel every believer is a priest with a place in God's house. Some take "nights" to mean seasons of trouble. Under the Gospel dispensation all the saints are priests, and they have a place in the house of the Lord; where they wait upon him in his ordinances, and serve him, and which they do continually. Some understand, by "nights", times of affliction, darkness, and desertion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-134.html Spurgeon applies it to dark times in church history: When night settles down on a church the Lord has his watchers and holy ones still guarding his truth https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps134.cfm Guzik's lesson is that praise must be added to service: doing the work is not enough. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-134/

**v. 2**
- **"Lift up your hands":** The Pulpit Commentary calls this the attitude of prayer and praise (Psalm 63:4; Psalm 119:48; Psalm 141:2) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/134.htm Calvin says the outward gesture exists to lift the heart: For why do men lift their hands when they pray? Is it not that their hates may be raised at the same time to God? https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-134.html
- **"Sanctuary": a translation question.** The Hebrew can be read two ways:
  - "Toward the holy place." The Pulpit Commentary and the Cambridge Bible prefer this, meaning toward the Holy of Holies.
  - "In holiness." Ellicott prefers this, because the priests were already standing in the sanctuary, and he links it to 1 Timothy 2:8, "lifting up holy hands."

  The usual meaning would be to the sanctuary (see reference above), but since the servants of Jehovah are here addressed as standing in the sanctuary, this direction seems unreasonable. Render, therefore, in holiness, and comp. "lifting up holy hands" (1Timothy 2:8). https://biblehub.com/psalms/134-2.htm
- Gill reports two Jewish readings. Aben Ezra took it as priests raising their hands to bless the people. Kimchi, whom Gill prefers, took it as hands raised to God in prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/134-2.htm
- Matthew Henry notes that priests washed before serving, and says this taught them to lift up holy hands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/134-2.html
- **Different emphases on raising hands today (not a formal split between denominations):**
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel, listed among the charismatic sites) treats it as a direct pattern for worship now: If God says we are to come to Him with hands raised up (Psalm 134:2), that is how we come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-11/
  - Calvin, as above, puts the weight on the raised heart that the gesture stands for. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-134.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary's homiletics section (R. Tuck) notes that in its own day outstretched hands were mainly used for the blessing, in the Catholic and Scottish Protestant churches. Tuck says the gesture could wisely be brought back into prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/134.htm

**v. 3**
- **Who gives the blessing?** Views differ:
  - **Gill:** These are not the priests blessing the people. More likely the servants are returning a blessing to whoever urged them to praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/134-3.html
  - **Clarke:** The priests and Levites are praying for the high priest as he goes to rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/134-1.html
  - **The Homilist (Biblical Illustrator):** The last verse seems to be the answer of the priests in dismissing the people with a blessing. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/134-1.htm
- **Link to the priestly blessing:** Guzik notes that most commentators see this as a reference to the priestly blessing described in Numbers 6:23-27. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-134/
- **"Maker of heaven and earth" and "from Zion":** Calvin says the two titles do different jobs. Calling God Creator shows his power. Zion shows he is near, so believers can come to him like children to a father. By looking to the heavens, then, they were to discover the power of God by looking to Zion, his dwellingplace, they were to recognize his fatherly love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-134.html Joseph Addison Alexander (in Spurgeon's notes) makes the same point: as Creator, God *can* bless; as the one who dwells in his church, he *will* bless. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps134.cfm
- **"You" is singular:** Guzik says this shows God blesses each believer personally. He adds that the blessing flows out from Zion to wherever God's people live. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-134/
- Matthew Henry says the blessings from Zion are spiritual, covenant blessings, and these are the best. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_134.cfm
- **Use in church services:** Bible Hub's summary notes that many congregations close evening services with Psalm 134 https://biblehub.com/psalms/134.htm

**Catholic and older-text readings**
- **Different numbering and wording:** The Douay-Rheims (following the ancient Greek and Latin Bibles) numbers this Psalm 133. Its verse 1 adds "in the courts of the house of our God," and "in the nights" moves to verse 2. Behold now bless ye the Lord, all ye servants of the Lord: Who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. 2{133:2}In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places, and bless ye the Lord. https://biblehub.com/drbc/psalms/134.htm Keil and Delitzsch see no reason to follow the Greek text in moving "in the nights." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/134-2.htm
- **Augustine (newadvent.org):**
  - v. 1: "Courts" are the wide spaces of a house. Whoever stands there is not cramped, and in that wideness can love even an enemy.
  - v. 2: "Night" means hard times. Blessing God by day, in good times, is easy. Job blessed God in his night of loss.
  - v. 3: God calls many to bless him but blesses "you" (one person), because he makes the many into one. Augustine ties this to the unity of Psalm 133.

  It is easy to bless by day. What is by day? In prosperity. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801134.htm
